findings.measured: Almost no content above 16 kHz; check whether an MP3/AAC or low-passed file was used as a source.

steps.text: Check the session for MP3 or AAC files, such as samples or imported references.
Look for a low-pass filter on the master or a bus cutting everything above 16 kHz.

findings.measured: Loudness range is 1.8 LU; there is little contrast between sections.

steps.text: Write volume automation (or use Clip Gain) so verses sit 2–3 dB below choruses.

other_options.text: Use Clip Gain on the verse clips so they sit 2–3 dB below the choruses.
Ease the mix-bus compressor: raise the threshold or slow the attack so transients get through.

notes.headline: This mix is technically clean and ready for mastering \u2014 the only two things worth a look are a missing top octave and very flat section-to-section dynamics.
notes.summary: Nothing here is broken: loudness sits at -17.08 LUFS with -4.15 dBTP true peak, so there's plenty of headroom for mastering, and the stereo picture holds up in mono (0.92 dB mono loss, 0.975 low-end correlation). Two things are flagged as informational. There's almost no content above 16 kHz, which usually means something in the chain is an MP3/AAC source or is being low-passed. And the loudness range is 1.8 LU, meaning your verses and choruses sit at nearly the same level.

priorities.title: Track down the missing top octave
priorities.why: Almost no content above 16 kHz normally points to a lossy source file or a low-pass somewhere in the chain. If it's an MP3 or AAC stem, mastering can't put that air back \u2014 better to catch it now while you can swap in the full-quality file.

priorities.title: Add contrast between sections
priorities.why: At 1.8 LU loudness range, the song stays at one level throughout. That can make choruses land flat on a listener, and mastering compression will flatten it further rather than restore the lift.

listen_for: On the chorus entries, does the song actually feel like it steps up, or just continues? Compare against a commercial track you like at matched level.
Cymbals and hi-hats on good headphones or monitors \u2014 do they sound dull or closed-off compared to what you expect from the source sounds?
If you find a low-pass or a lossy file, A/B the fixed version against this bounce to confirm the top end returns.
strengths: True peak at -4.15 dBTP and -17.08 LUFS integrated leaves clean headroom for mastering.
Low-end correlation of 0.975 \u2014 your bass is solid and centered, no phase trouble down low.
Left/right balance within -0.4 dB and only 0.92 dB mono loss, so the mix translates well on mono systems.

judge.priority_order: F1 (info, potentially unfixable if lossy source) is placed first over F2 (info, fixable dynamics issue), a reasonable severity-tied prioritization by audible consequence.
judge.explains_impact: F1's why explains mastering can't restore lost air, and F2's why explains choruses will 'land flat on a listener,' both describing listening impact not just numbers.
judge.groups_causes: The two findings (missing top octave vs. flat dynamics) are unrelated causes and are correctly kept as separate priorities rather than merged.
judge.specific: Notes cite actual measurements (-17.08 LUFS, -4.15 dBTP, 0.975 low-end correlation, 1.8 LU) and reference this bounce's specific findings rather than generic advice.
judge.stage_appropriate: Notes correctly frame the mix as having 'plenty of headroom for mastering' rather than judging it against release loudness standards, matching the mix stage.
judge.faithful: All cited measurements and claims (headroom, mono loss, low-end correlation, LRA, missing high end) match the report exactly with no invented issues.
judge.concise: The notes are compact, with a short headline, summary, two priorities, and brief strengths list without repetition or hype.
